The verse runs almost word for word with 2 Kgs 16:5, the Kings account of the Syro-Ephraimite war (c. 734–732 BCE). One difference is that Isaiah has the singular *wᵉlōʾ yāḵōl* “and he could not,” where Kings has the plural *wᵉlōʾ yāḵᵉlû*. The translation keeps ASV “but could not prevail against it,” which leaves the subject unexpressed and gives the sense of *lᵉhillāḥēm ʿālêhā*, literally “to fight against it,” picking up *lammilḥāmāh ʿālêhā* “to war against it” earlier in the verse. NRSV “but could not mount an attack against it” is an alternative reading of the same infinitive.

*ʾărām* is “Aram,” the Aramean kingdom of Damascus, with NRSV and NJPS. ASV's “Syria” follows the Greek and Latin tradition, which uses the later name (overlay `aram-names-isaiah`).

paragraphs.text: וַיֻּגַּ֗ד לְבֵ֤ית דָּוִד֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר נָ֥חָֽה אֲרָ֖ם עַל־אֶפְרָ֑יִם וַיָּ֤נַע לְבָבוֹ֙ וּלְבַ֣ב עַמּ֔וֹ כְּנ֥וֹעַ עֲצֵי־יַ֖עַר מִפְּנֵי־רֽוּחַ׃

i18n.en: And it was told the house of David, saying: “Aram is confederate with Ephraim.” And his heart trembled, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the forest tremble before the wind.
i18n.he: וַיֻּגַּ֗ד לְבֵ֤ית דָּוִד֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר נָ֥חָֽה אֲרָ֖ם עַל־אֶפְרָ֑יִם וַיָּ֤נַע לְבָבוֹ֙ וּלְבַ֣ב עַמּ֔וֹ כְּנ֥וֹעַ עֲצֵי־יַ֖עַר מִפְּנֵי־רֽוּחַ׃

notes.official:
*nāḥāh ʾărām ʿal-ʾep̄rāyim* is literally “Aram has come to rest upon Ephraim.” The verb *nûaḥ* “rest, settle” is read by ASV (“is confederate with”) and NRSV (“has allied itself with”) as a political alliance. Other readers take it in its physical sense, troops “encamped in” Ephraimite territory. The translation keeps ASV. The same verb returns in 7:19, where the swarms of the fly and the bee “settle” on the land.

“The house of David” is the dynasty, so “his heart” is Ahaz's. The simile plays on one verb: *wayyānaʿ* “trembled” and *kᵉnôaʿ* “as … tremble” are both from *nûaʿ* “shake, sway.”

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָה֮ אֶֽל־יְשַׁעְיָהוּ֒ צֵא־נָא֙ לִקְרַ֣את אָחָ֔ז אַתָּ֕ה וּשְׁאָ֖ר יָשׁ֣וּב בְּנֶ֑ךָ אֶל־קְצֵ֗ה תְּעָלַת֙ הַבְּרֵכָ֣ה הָעֶלְיוֹנָ֔ה אֶל־מְסִלַּ֖ת שְׂדֵ֥ה כוֹבֵֽס׃

i18n.en: Then YHWH said to Isaiah: “Go out now to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway of the fuller’s field,
i18n.he: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָה֮ אֶֽל־יְשַׁעְיָהוּ֒ צֵא־נָא֙ לִקְרַ֣את אָחָ֔ז אַתָּ֕ה וּשְׁאָ֖ר יָשׁ֣וּב בְּנֶ֑ךָ אֶל־קְצֵ֗ה תְּעָלַת֙ הַבְּרֵכָ֣ה הָעֶלְיוֹנָ֔ה אֶל־מְסִלַּ֖ת שְׂדֵ֥ה כוֹבֵֽס׃

notes.official:
*šᵉʾār yāšûḇ* “a remnant will return” is the name of Isaiah's son. As with ASV, NRSV and NJPS, it is transliterated, “Shear-jashub,” and its meaning is given here (overlay `sign-names-isaiah-7-8`). The name can be read two ways. As a threat, *only* a remnant will return; as a promise, a remnant *will* return. The verb *šûḇ* is also open between “come back” and “turn back” in repentance. In 10:21–22 the same two words recur as a clause, “A remnant will return … to the Mighty God,” which takes the repentance sense. The noun is *šᵉʾār*, not *šᵉʾērîṯ*; the central `she-erit-remnant-cross-corpus-theological-keyword` is not applied.

The boy's presence is part of the message: 8:18 calls the prophet's children “signs and portents in Israel.” The meeting place, “the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway of the fuller's field,” is the same spot where the Rabshakeh later stands (36:2; 2 Kgs 18:17).

paragraphs.text: וְאָמַרְתָּ֣ אֵ֠לָיו הִשָּׁמֵ֨ר וְהַשְׁקֵ֜ט אַל־תִּירָ֗א וּלְבָבְךָ֙ אַל־יֵרַ֔ךְ מִשְּׁנֵ֨י זַנְב֧וֹת הָאוּדִ֛ים הָעֲשֵׁנִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה בָּחֳרִי־אַ֛ף רְצִ֥ין וַאֲרָ֖ם וּבֶן־רְמַלְיָֽהוּ׃

i18n.en: and say to him: Take heed, and be quiet; do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two tails of smoking firebrands, because of the fierce anger of Rezin and Aram, and of the son of Remaliah.
i18n.he: וְאָמַרְתָּ֣ אֵ֠לָיו הִשָּׁמֵ֨ר וְהַשְׁקֵ֜ט אַל־תִּירָ֗א וּלְבָבְךָ֙ אַל־יֵרַ֔ךְ מִשְּׁנֵ֨י זַנְב֧וֹת הָאוּדִ֛ים הָעֲשֵׁנִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה בָּחֳרִי־אַ֛ף רְצִ֥ין וַאֲרָ֖ם וּבֶן־רְמַלְיָֽהוּ׃

notes.official: *zanḇôṯ hāʾûḏîm hāʿăšēnîm* “tails of smoking firebrands” (ASV) are the charred stubs of sticks pulled from a fire, which still smoke but are nearly burnt out. The image belittles Rezin and Pekah. Pekah is not named; he is “the son of Remaliah,” here and in 7:5, 9. The instruction *hiššāmēr wᵉhašqēṭ* “take heed, and be quiet” anticipates *bᵉhašqēṭ* “in quietness” of 30:15. “Aram” replaces ASV “Syria” (`aram-names-isaiah`).

paragraphs.text: יַ֗עַן כִּֽי־יָעַ֥ץ עָלֶ֛יךָ אֲרָ֖ם רָעָ֑ה אֶפְרַ֥יִם וּבֶן־רְמַלְיָ֖הוּ לֵאמֹֽר׃

i18n.en: Because Aram has planned evil against you — Ephraim and the son of Remaliah — saying:
i18n.he: יַ֗עַן כִּֽי־יָעַ֥ץ עָלֶ֛יךָ אֲרָ֖ם רָעָ֑ה אֶפְרַ֥יִם וּבֶן־רְמַלְיָ֖הוּ לֵאמֹֽר׃

paragraphs.text: נַעֲלֶ֤ה בִֽיהוּדָה֙ וּנְקִיצֶ֔נָּה וְנַבְקִעֶ֖נָּה אֵלֵ֑ינוּ וְנַמְלִ֥יךְ מֶ֙לֶךְ֙ בְּתוֹכָ֔הּ אֵ֖ת בֶּן־טָֽבְאַֽל׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us break into it for ourselves, and set up a king in its midst, the son of Tabeel;
i18n.he: נַעֲלֶ֤ה בִֽיהוּדָה֙ וּנְקִיצֶ֔נָּה וְנַבְקִעֶ֖נָּה אֵלֵ֑ינוּ וְנַמְלִ֥יךְ מֶ֙לֶךְ֙ בְּתוֹכָ֔הּ אֵ֖ת בֶּן־טָֽבְאַֽל׃ (ס)

notes.official:
*nᵉqîṣennāh* is the most uncertain word of the verse. The translation reads it as the Hiphil of *qûṣ* I “feel dread, loathing,” giving “and terrify it.” BDB gives this parse (“let us cause her sickening dread”) but calls it weak and recommends reading *nᵉṣîqennāh*, from *ṣûq* “distress, press hard.” Either way the sense is one of pressure and terror, which is why “terrify” is kept. The same root returns in 7:16, “whose two kings you dread.” ASV “vex it” takes the same root more weakly. NRSV “cut off Judah” derives the form from a root meaning “cut, tear apart.” Because the root is disputed, the decision is recorded as inferred (overlay `qutz-dread-isaiah-7`).

“The son of Tabeel,” the coalition's candidate for the throne, is otherwise unknown. The name means “God is good” (*ṭāḇ ʾēl*). The Masoretic pointing *ṭāḇᵉʾal*, for *ṭāḇᵉʾēl* (Ezra 4:7), is explained in two ways. Some take it simply as a pausal form (Olshausen, König). More often it is read as a deliberate pun on *ṭāḇ* and *ʾal*, “good-for-nothing” (Delitzsch, Dillmann, Duhm, Stade; BDB s.v.). The line keeps the conventional name.

paragraphs.text: כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֖ר אֲדֹנָ֣י יְהוִ֑ה לֹ֥א תָק֖וּם וְלֹ֥א תִֽהְיֶֽה׃

i18n.en: thus says the Lord YHWH: It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass.
i18n.he: כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֖ר אֲדֹנָ֣י יְהוִ֑ה לֹ֥א תָק֖וּם וְלֹ֥א תִֽהְיֶֽה׃

paragraphs.text: כִּ֣י רֹ֤אשׁ אֲרָם֙ דַּמֶּ֔שֶׂק וְרֹ֥אשׁ דַּמֶּ֖שֶׂק רְצִ֑ין וּבְע֗וֹד שִׁשִּׁ֤ים וְחָמֵשׁ֙ שָׁנָ֔ה יֵחַ֥ת אֶפְרַ֖יִם מֵעָֽם׃

i18n.en: For the head of Aram is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin; and within sixty-five years Ephraim shall be shattered, so that it is no longer a people.
i18n.he: כִּ֣י רֹ֤אשׁ אֲרָם֙ דַּמֶּ֔שֶׂק וְרֹ֥אשׁ דַּמֶּ֖שֶׂק רְצִ֑ין וּבְע֗וֹד שִׁשִּׁ֤ים וְחָמֵשׁ֙ שָׁנָ֔ה יֵחַ֥ת אֶפְרַ֖יִם מֵעָֽם׃

notes.official: The clause “and within sixty-five years Ephraim shall be shattered, so that it is no longer a people” breaks the parallel “the head of … is …” sequence of 7:8a and 9a. Many commentators take it as a later gloss, and some move it after 7:9a; NJPS prints it there, with a note that it has been moved down from v. 8. Samaria fell in 722 BCE, about twelve years after the crisis. Sixty-five years from the crisis reaches the reign of Esarhaddon (681–669 BCE), and the gloss is often linked to the later resettlement of the north (Ezra 4:2, 10). The line translates the Masoretic Text in its received order and leaves the gloss hypothesis to this note (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

paragraphs.text: וְרֹ֤אשׁ אֶפְרַ֙יִם֙ שֹׁמְר֔וֹן וְרֹ֥אשׁ שֹׁמְר֖וֹן בֶּן־רְמַלְיָ֑הוּ אִ֚ם לֹ֣א תַאֲמִ֔ינוּ כִּ֖י לֹ֥א תֵאָמֵֽנוּ׃ (ס)

i18n.en: And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established.”
i18n.he: וְרֹ֤אשׁ אֶפְרַ֙יִם֙ שֹׁמְר֔וֹן וְרֹ֥אשׁ שֹׁמְר֖וֹן בֶּן־רְמַלְיָ֑הוּ אִ֚ם לֹ֣א תַאֲמִ֔ינוּ כִּ֖י לֹ֥א תֵאָמֵֽנוּ׃ (ס)

notes.official:
The oracle ends on a play on the root *ʾmn*: *ʾim lōʾ ṯaʾămînû kî lōʾ ṯēʾāmēnû*. The Hiphil *taʾămînû* is “believe, trust,” to hold firm on something. The Niphal *tēʾāmēnû* is “be made firm, be established.” The Niphal is the verb of the dynastic promise to David, *wᵉneʾman bêṯᵉḵā* “your house shall be made sure” (2 Sam 7:16). Both verbs are plural: the warning is to the house of David, not to Ahaz alone.

The translation keeps ASV “If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established,” taking *kî* as asseverative. NRSV imitates the pun, “If you do not stand firm in faith, you shall not stand at all.” Others take *kî* as causal. English cannot reproduce the root-play without changing one of the two senses, so it is explained here and not imitated in the line.

paragraphs.text: וַיּ֣וֹסֶף יְהוָ֔ה דַּבֵּ֥ר אֶל־אָחָ֖ז לֵאמֹֽר׃

i18n.en: And YHWH spoke again to Ahaz, saying:
i18n.he: וַיּ֣וֹסֶף יְהוָ֔ה דַּבֵּ֥ר אֶל־אָחָ֖ז לֵאמֹֽר׃

paragraphs.text: שְׁאַל־לְךָ֣ א֔וֹת מֵעִ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֑יךָ הַעְמֵ֣ק שְׁאָ֔לָה א֖וֹ הַגְבֵּ֥הַּ לְמָֽעְלָה׃

i18n.en: “Ask for yourself a sign from YHWH your God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.”
i18n.he: שְׁאַל־לְךָ֣ א֔וֹת מֵעִ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֑יךָ הַעְמֵ֣ק שְׁאָ֔לָה א֖וֹ הַגְבֵּ֥הַּ לְמָֽעְלָה׃

notes.official: *haʿmēq šᵉʾālāh ʾô hagbēah lᵉmāʿᵉlāh* is a merism: the sign may come from anywhere between the depths and the heights. The Masoretic pointing *šᵉʾālāh* is the emphatic imperative “ask!” and the translation follows it with ASV, “ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.” Many modern readers repoint the consonants as *šᵉʾōlāh* “to Sheol,” which gives a cleaner antithesis. NRSV adopts this (“let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven”), and so does NJPS (“anywhere down to Sheol or up to the sky”). The Vulgate's *in profundum inferni* reflects the same reading. The repointing is reported and not adopted (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`), so the central `sheol-underworld-realm-of-the-dead` entry does not apply here. YHWH is “your God” to Ahaz in this verse; contrast “my God” in 7:13.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אָחָ֑ז לֹא־אֶשְׁאַ֥ל וְלֹֽא־אֲנַסֶּ֖ה אֶת־יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: But Ahaz said: “I will not ask, and I will not test YHWH.”
i18n.he: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אָחָ֑ז לֹא־אֶשְׁאַ֥ל וְלֹֽא־אֲנַסֶּ֖ה אֶת־יְהוָֽה׃

notes.official: *wᵉlōʾ-ʾănasseh ʾeṯ-YHWH* “and I will not test YHWH” uses the Piel of *nsh*, “test, put to the proof.” ASV has “tempt.” Ahaz's refusal is worded in the language of Deut 6:16, “You shall not put YHWH your God to the test.” His answer is formally pious, but 7:13 treats it as a refusal to trust. The central `nisah-divine-testing` entry (“tested”) is extended to cover the reverse case, a human being testing God (Exod 17:2, 7; Deut 6:16).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר שִׁמְעוּ־נָ֖א בֵּ֣ית דָּוִ֑ד הַמְעַ֤ט מִכֶּם֙ הַלְא֣וֹת אֲנָשִׁ֔ים כִּ֥י תַלְא֖וּ גַּ֥ם אֶת־אֱלֹהָֽי׃

i18n.en: And he said: “Hear now, O house of David: Is it too small a thing for you to weary men, that you will weary my God also?
i18n.he: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר שִׁמְעוּ־נָ֖א בֵּ֣ית דָּוִ֑ד הַמְעַ֤ט מִכֶּם֙ הַלְא֣וֹת אֲנָשִׁ֔ים כִּ֥י תַלְא֖וּ גַּ֥ם אֶת־אֱלֹהָֽי׃

notes.official: The address is plural, “O house of David,” like the verbs of 7:9. *halʾôṯ ʾănāšîm* “to weary men” contrasts human beings with God; ʾănāšîm is generic here, and NRSV renders it “mortals.” The line keeps ASV. The prophet now says “my God,” where in 7:11 he had said to Ahaz “YHWH your God.”

paragraphs.text: לָ֠כֵן יִתֵּ֨ן אֲדֹנָ֥י ה֛וּא לָכֶ֖ם א֑וֹת הִנֵּ֣ה הָעַלְמָ֗ה הָרָה֙ וְיֹלֶ֣דֶת בֵּ֔ן וְקָרָ֥את שְׁמ֖וֹ עִמָּ֥נוּ אֵֽל׃

i18n.en: Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
i18n.he: לָ֠כֵן יִתֵּ֨ן אֲדֹנָ֥י ה֛וּא לָכֶ֖ם א֑וֹת הִנֵּ֣ה הָעַלְמָ֗ה הָרָה֙ וְיֹלֶ֣דֶת בֵּ֔ן וְקָרָ֥את שְׁמ֖וֹ עִמָּ֥נוּ אֵֽל׃

notes.official:
*hā-ʿalmâ* is rendered “the young woman,” with NRSV and NJPS, and not “a virgin,” with ASV and KJV (overlay `almah-young-woman-isaiah-7-14`). *ʿalmâ* is the feminine of *ʿelem* “young man” (1 Sam 17:56; 20:22). It denotes a young woman of marriageable age and does not itself specify virginity (BDB, HALOT s.v.). Its other occurrences are Gen 24:43 (Rebekah at the well), Exod 2:8 (Moses' sister), Ps 68:26 (Heb.), Prov 30:19 (“the way of a man with a young woman”), and Song 1:3 and 6:8. In Song 6:8 the *ʿălāmôṯ* stand beside queens and concubines.

The word that usually carries the sense of virginity is *bᵉṯûlâ* (Lev 21:13–14; Deut 22:23–29). Even that word is sometimes qualified: Gen 24:16 adds “whom no man had known,” and Joel 1:8 has a *bᵉṯûlâ* mourning “the husband of her youth.” On the other side, it is often observed that no biblical occurrence of *ʿalmâ* clearly refers to a married woman. The translation does not depend on that point, because it renders what the word denotes rather than what it might exclude.

The article makes her definite, “the young woman”: a woman the speaker and his hearers could identify. Proposed identifications include the wife of Ahaz (and so the mother of Hezekiah), the prophet's own wife (“the prophetess,” 8:3), and an unnamed woman at court. The line does not decide among them.

The grammar fixes the time of the sign. *hārâ* is the adjective “pregnant,” not a future verb, and *yōleḏeṯ* is a participle, “about to bear.” The same formula is spoken to Hagar, who is already pregnant (Gen 16:4, 11: *hinnāḵ hārâ wᵉyōlaḏt bēn wᵉqārāʾṯ šᵉmô*). It is also spoken to Manoah's wife, who has been barren (Judg 13:3, 5), so in an annunciation the adjective can also look ahead. The line follows NRSV, “is with child and shall bear a son”; ASV's “shall conceive” is the prospective reading.

*wᵉqārāʾṯ* is either the 2fs perfect “and you shall call,” as in Gen 16:11, or an older 3fs form, “and she shall call.” No woman is addressed in 7:14, where the addressees are the house of David (*lāḵem*, plural), so the line reads “and shall call,” with the young woman as subject (NRSV “and shall name him”). Matthew 1:23 has the third plural, “and they shall call.” The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) is reported to read *wqrʾ* “and he (one) shall call.” That reading was not verified for this edition. The Septuagint has the second person, *kaléseis* “you shall call” (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

*ʿimmānû ʾēl* “with us is God” is transliterated as a name, “Immanuel,” as in ASV, NRSV and NJPS (overlay `sign-names-isaiah-7-8`). It recurs at 8:8 as a vocative (“O Immanuel”) and at 8:10 as a clause (“for God is with us”). Like Shear-jashub (7:3) and Maher-shalal-hash-baz (8:1, 3), it is a sentence-name that carries a message. *ʾôṯ* “a sign” is the plain noun. The sign Ahaz refused to ask for (7:11–12) is given unasked, and the timetable of 7:15–16 ties it to the near future of the crisis.

**Reception.** The Septuagint renders *hā-ʿalmâ* by *hē parthenos* (*idou hē parthenos en gastri hexei … kai kaleseis to onoma autou Emmanouēl*). In Greek the word usually means “virgin,” but it can also mean a young unmarried woman: LXX Gen 34:3 calls Dinah *parthenos* after the rape of 34:2. Aquila and Theodotion are reported to have put *neanis* “young woman” (Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 3.21.1), and the dispute appears already in Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho* (e.g. 43; 67). Matthew 1:23 cites the Greek form, “Behold, the virgin shall be with child … and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” and applies it to the conception of Jesus. The project's Matthew line follows the Septuagint that Matthew cites (central `isa-7-14-virgin-birth-mt-1-22-23-parthenos-vs-almah-philological-dispute-cross-corpus`). The Isaiah line renders the Hebrew. The two lines differ because each translates its own source.

**Wheel of Heaven reading (speculative; commentary only).** The project's canon reads the conception in Matthew 1:18–20 as the birth of “a child issued from a woman and from one of their own,” one of the creators (*The Book Which Tells the Truth*, 4:3). The canon does not cite Isaiah 7:14 at that point. Carrying that reading back to this verse goes through Matthew's Greek citation, not through the Hebrew. The Hebrew says nothing about how the child is conceived, and this reading has no effect on the line.

paragraphs.text: חֶמְאָ֥ה וּדְבַ֖שׁ יֹאכֵ֑ל לְדַעְתּ֛וֹ מָא֥וֹס בָּרָ֖ע וּבָח֥וֹר בַּטּֽוֹב׃

i18n.en: Curds and honey he shall eat, when he knows to refuse the evil and choose the good.
i18n.he: חֶמְאָ֥ה וּדְבַ֖שׁ יֹאכֵ֑ל לְדַעְתּ֛וֹ מָא֥וֹס בָּרָ֖ע וּבָח֥וֹר בַּטּֽוֹב׃

notes.official:
*ḥemʾâ* is “curds,” soured or curdled milk (BDB “curd”; NRSV, NJPS), here and twice in 7:22. ASV's “butter” is replaced (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-7`). Curds and honey are pastoral food, which needs no tilled fields. Whether the diet signals plenty or the reduced economy of a land laid waste is argued both ways; 7:21–25 describes a land returned to pasture.

*lᵉḏaʿtô* is read temporally, “when he knows” (ASV; NRSV “by the time he knows how”). The purposive reading, “that he may know,” is also possible. “To refuse the evil and choose the good” marks the age of moral discernment (cf. Deut 1:39, the children “who do not know good and evil”). The central `tov-ra-merism` (“from good to bad,” the Gen 31 idiom) is not applied.

paragraphs.text: כִּ֠י בְּטֶ֨רֶם יֵדַ֥ע הַנַּ֛עַר מָאֹ֥ס בָּרָ֖ע וּבָחֹ֣ר בַּטּ֑וֹב תֵּעָזֵ֤ב הָאֲדָמָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אַתָּ֣ה קָ֔ץ מִפְּנֵ֖י שְׁנֵ֥י מְלָכֶֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: For before the child knows to refuse the evil and choose the good, the ground whose two kings you dread shall be forsaken.
i18n.he: כִּ֠י בְּטֶ֨רֶם יֵדַ֥ע הַנַּ֛עַר מָאֹ֥ס בָּרָ֖ע וּבָחֹ֣ר בַּטּ֑וֹב תֵּעָזֵ֤ב הָאֲדָמָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אַתָּ֣ה קָ֔ץ מִפְּנֵ֖י שְׁנֵ֥י מְלָכֶֽיהָ׃

notes.official: *ʾăšer ʾattāh qāṣ mippᵉnê šᵉnê mᵉlāḵêhā* is “whose two kings you dread.” The idiom *qûṣ mippᵉnê* means “be in dread of,” as in Exod 1:12 (Egypt and the Israelites) and Num 22:3 (Moab and Israel). ASV's “abhor” is replaced, and the verb now matches 7:6 (overlay `qutz-dread-isaiah-7`). The two kings are Rezin and Pekah. Damascus fell to Tiglath-pileser III in 732 BCE, and Pekah was killed about the same time (2 Kgs 15:29–30; 16:9). *hā-ʾăḏāmāh* is “the ground,” here the territory of the two kingdoms, under the central `adam-adamah` entry as at 1:7 and 14:1–2.

paragraphs.text: יָבִ֨יא יְהוָ֜ה עָלֶ֗יךָ וְעַֽל־עַמְּךָ֮ וְעַל־בֵּ֣ית אָבִיךָ֒ יָמִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא־בָ֔אוּ לְמִיּ֥וֹם סוּר־אֶפְרַ֖יִם מֵעַ֣ל יְהוּדָ֑ה אֵ֖ת מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃ (פ)

i18n.en: YHWH will bring upon you, and upon your people, and upon your father’s house, days that have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah — even the king of Assyria.”
i18n.he: יָבִ֨יא יְהוָ֜ה עָלֶ֗יךָ וְעַֽל־עַמְּךָ֮ וְעַל־בֵּ֣ית אָבִיךָ֒ יָמִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא־בָ֔אוּ לְמִיּ֥וֹם סוּר־אֶפְרַ֖יִם מֵעַ֣ל יְהוּדָ֑ה אֵ֖ת מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר׃ (פ)

notes.official: “Days that have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah” points back to the division of the kingdom after Solomon (1 Kgs 12). The closing *ʾēṯ meleḵ ʾaššûr* “even the king of Assyria” stands loosely at the end of the verse, marked only by the object marker. Many commentators take it as an explanatory gloss, like *bᵉmeleḵ ʾaššûr* in 7:20. The Masoretic Text is kept in the line (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

paragraphs.text: וְהָיָ֣ה ׀ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא יִשְׁרֹ֤ק יְהוָה֙ לַזְּב֔וּב אֲשֶׁ֥ר בִּקְצֵ֖ה יְאֹרֵ֣י מִצְרָ֑יִם וְלַ֨דְּבוֹרָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּאֶ֥רֶץ אַשּֽׁוּר׃

i18n.en: And it shall come to pass in that day that YHWH will whistle for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.
i18n.he: וְהָיָ֣ה ׀ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא יִשְׁרֹ֤ק יְהוָה֙ לַזְּב֔וּב אֲשֶׁ֥ר בִּקְצֵ֖ה יְאֹרֵ֣י מִצְרָ֑יִם וְלַ֨דְּבוֹרָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּאֶ֥רֶץ אַשּֽׁוּר׃

notes.official: *yišrōq* is “will whistle,” with NRSV and NJPS and as at 5:26, where the same verb calls the distant nation. ASV's “hiss” is replaced. *šāraq* is the summoning whistle here; where it expresses scorn (Jer 19:8; Lam 2:15) it is “hiss” (overlay `sharaq-whistle-isaiah`). The fly and the bee are collective singulars and are rendered literally; the context, not the words, makes them armies. *yᵉʾōrê miṣrāyim* is the plural of the Egyptian loanword *yᵉʾōr* “the Nile,” its branches and channels: “the rivers of Egypt” (ASV; central `yeor-nile-egyptian-loanword`; NRSV “the sources of the streams of Egypt”).

paragraphs.text: וּבָ֨אוּ וְנָח֤וּ כֻלָּם֙ בְּנַחֲלֵ֣י הַבַּתּ֔וֹת וּבִנְקִיקֵ֖י הַסְּלָעִ֑ים וּבְכֹל֙ הַנַּ֣עֲצוּצִ֔ים וּבְכֹ֖ל הַנַּהֲלֹלִֽים׃

i18n.en: And they shall come, and shall settle, all of them, in the desolate valleys, and in the clefts of the rocks, and on all the thorn-hedges, and on all the pastures.
i18n.he: וּבָ֨אוּ וְנָח֤וּ כֻלָּם֙ בְּנַחֲלֵ֣י הַבַּתּ֔וֹת וּבִנְקִיקֵ֖י הַסְּלָעִ֑ים וּבְכֹל֙ הַנַּ֣עֲצוּצִ֔ים וּבְכֹ֖ל הַנַּהֲלֹלִֽים׃

notes.official: The verse has three rare words. *naḥălê habbattôṯ* “the desolate valleys” (ASV) uses a noun known only here, connected with *bāṯāh* “a waste” of 5:6; modern versions have “steep ravines.” *naʿăṣûṣîm* “thorn-hedges” recurs at 55:13. *nahălōlîm*, also known only here, is “pastures” in ASV; others derive it from *nhl* “lead to water” and render “watering places.” The translation follows ASV for all three. The verb *nāḥû* is “settle” (ASV “rest”), which keeps the swarm image concrete and is the same verb as 7:2.

paragraphs.text: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֡וּא יְגַלַּ֣ח אֲדֹנָי֩ בְּתַ֨עַר הַשְּׂכִירָ֜ה בְּעֶבְרֵ֤י נָהָר֙ בְּמֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר אֶת־הָרֹ֖אשׁ וְשַׂ֣עַר הָרַגְלָ֑יִם וְגַ֥ם אֶת־הַזָּקָ֖ן תִּסְפֶּֽה׃ (ס)

i18n.en: In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired in the parts beyond the River — with the king of Assyria — the head and the hair of the feet; and it shall also consume the beard.
i18n.he: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֡וּא יְגַלַּ֣ח אֲדֹנָי֩ בְּתַ֨עַר הַשְּׂכִירָ֜ה בְּעֶבְרֵ֤י נָהָר֙ בְּמֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר אֶת־הָרֹ֖אשׁ וְשַׂ֣עַר הָרַגְלָ֑יִם וְגַ֥ם אֶת־הַזָּקָ֖ן תִּסְפֶּֽה׃ (ס)

notes.official:
The razor is *taʿar haśśᵉḵîrāh* “a razor that is hired” (ASV). The image is ironic: Ahaz had hired Assyria with silver and gold from the temple and the palace (2 Kgs 16:7–8), and the hired blade will be turned on Judah. *bᵉʿeḇrê nāhār* is “in the parts beyond the River,” the Euphrates. The phrase *bᵉmeleḵ ʾaššûr* “with the king of Assyria” identifies the razor and is often taken as a gloss, like the end of 7:17. It is kept in the line (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

Shaving was a humiliation (cf. 2 Sam 10:4). *śaʿar hāraḡlāyim* “the hair of the feet” is a euphemism for the pubic hair, since “feet” serves as a euphemism elsewhere (e.g. Judg 3:24; 1 Sam 24:4). The line keeps the Hebrew expression rather than explaining it. *tispeh* “it shall consume” (from *sph* “sweep away”) has the razor as its subject.

paragraphs.text: וְהָיָ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא יְחַיֶּה־אִ֛ישׁ עֶגְלַ֥ת בָּקָ֖ר וּשְׁתֵּי־צֹֽאן׃

i18n.en: And it shall come to pass in that day that a man shall keep alive a young cow and two sheep;
i18n.he: וְהָיָ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא יְחַיֶּה־אִ֛ישׁ עֶגְלַ֥ת בָּקָ֖ר וּשְׁתֵּי־צֹֽאן׃

paragraphs.text: וְהָיָ֗ה מֵרֹ֛ב עֲשׂ֥וֹת חָלָ֖ב יֹאכַ֣ל חֶמְאָ֑ה כִּֽי־חֶמְאָ֤ה וּדְבַשׁ֙ יֹאכֵ֔ל כָּל־הַנּוֹתָ֖ר בְּקֶ֥רֶב הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: and it shall come to pass that, because of the abundance of milk that they give, he shall eat curds; for curds and honey shall everyone eat who is left in the midst of the land.
i18n.he: וְהָיָ֗ה מֵרֹ֛ב עֲשׂ֥וֹת חָלָ֖ב יֹאכַ֣ל חֶמְאָ֑ה כִּֽי־חֶמְאָ֤ה וּדְבַשׁ֙ יֹאכֵ֔ל כָּל־הַנּוֹתָ֖ר בְּקֶ֥רֶב הָאָֽרֶץ׃

notes.official: “Because of the abundance of milk” describes a land with few people and few animals. The young cow and two sheep of 7:21 give more milk than the survivors need, so “everyone who is left” (*kol-hannôṯār*) lives on curds and honey. *ḥemʾâ* is “curds,” as in 7:15. The line keeps ASV's wording otherwise and leaves open whether the diet is plenty or poverty.

paragraphs.text: וְהָיָה֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא יִֽהְיֶ֣ה כָל־מָק֗וֹם אֲשֶׁ֧ר יִֽהְיֶה־שָּׁ֛ם אֶ֥לֶף גֶּ֖פֶן בְּאֶ֣לֶף כָּ֑סֶף לַשָּׁמִ֥יר וְלַשַּׁ֖יִת יִֽהְיֶֽה׃

i18n.en: And it shall come to pass in that day that every place where there were a thousand vines, at a thousand pieces of silver, shall be for briers and thorns.
i18n.he: וְהָיָה֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא יִֽהְיֶ֣ה כָל־מָק֗וֹם אֲשֶׁ֧ר יִֽהְיֶה־שָּׁ֛ם אֶ֥לֶף גֶּ֖פֶן בְּאֶ֣לֶף כָּ֑סֶף לַשָּׁמִ֥יר וְלַשַּׁ֖יִת יִֽהְיֶֽה׃

paragraphs.text: בַּחִצִּ֥ים וּבַקֶּ֖שֶׁת יָ֣בוֹא שָׁ֑מָּה כִּי־שָׁמִ֥יר וָשַׁ֖יִת תִּֽהְיֶ֥ה כָל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: With arrows and with bow shall one come there, for all the land shall be briers and thorns.
i18n.he: בַּחִצִּ֥ים וּבַקֶּ֖שֶׁת יָ֣בוֹא שָׁ֑מָּה כִּי־שָׁמִ֥יר וָשַׁ֖יִת תִּֽהְיֶ֥ה כָל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

paragraphs.text: וְכֹ֣ל הֶהָרִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר בַּמַּעְדֵּר֙ יֵעָ֣דֵר֔וּן לֹֽא־תָב֣וֹא שָׁ֔מָּה יִרְאַ֖ת שָׁמִ֣יר וָשָׁ֑יִת וְהָיָה֙ לְמִשְׁלַ֣ח שׁ֔וֹר וּלְמִרְמַ֖ס שֶֽׂה׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And as for all the hills that were hoed with the hoe, you shall not come there for fear of briers and thorns; but it shall be for the sending forth of oxen and for the treading of sheep.
i18n.he: וְכֹ֣ל הֶהָרִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר בַּמַּעְדֵּר֙ יֵעָ֣דֵר֔וּן לֹֽא־תָב֣וֹא שָׁ֔מָּה יִרְאַ֖ת שָׁמִ֣יר וָשָׁ֑יִת וְהָיָה֙ לְמִשְׁלַ֣ח שׁ֔וֹר וּלְמִרְמַ֖ס שֶֽׂה׃ (פ)

notes.official: *lōʾ-ṯāḇôʾ šāmmāh yirʾaṯ šāmîr wāšāyiṯ* can be construed two ways. Taken as second person, it means “you shall not come there for fear of briers and thorns” (ASV, NRSV), with *yirʾaṯ* as an adverbial accusative. Taken as third feminine, with *yirʾaṯ* as subject, it means “the fear of briers and thorns shall not come there,” so that the hoed hills are spared the thorns. The line keeps ASV. The second construal is the one NJPS adopts (“the perils of thornbush and thistle shall not spread to any of the hills”). *bammaʿdēr yēʿāḏērûn* is “hoed with the hoe,” matching *yēʿāḏēr* “hoed” in the Song of the Vineyard (5:6). ASV has “digged with the mattock.”
